explain.say: Fourteen lines. That is all a sonnet is, and poets have squeezed love, grief, faith and fury into that small box for about eight hundred years. The timeline follows the sonnet from a royal court in Sicily, through Petrarch and Shakespeare, to poets writing it today.

explain.say: Start with Petrarch, an Italian poet who wrote hundreds of poems to a woman called Laura. His sonnet has two parts: an octave of eight lines that sets out a problem or desire, then a turn, called the volta, at line nine, and a sestet of six lines that answers or shifts. Can you feel how a turn makes a poem think?

explain.say: Why change it? Italian is full of rhymes; English has fewer. So when Wyatt and Surrey brought the sonnet over in the 1500s, Surrey settled on three quatrains and a couplet, which needs more, easier rhymes. Shakespeare made that form famous. Which do you prefer: a slow turn, or a final punch?

explain.say: Then poets bent it to new purposes. Milton wrote sonnets on politics and on his blindness. Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote a whole sequence of love sonnets, asking how do I love thee, and counting the ways. In 1919 Claude McKay, in Harlem, made the sonnet a cry of defiance against racist mobs. Why might a protest poet choose such a strict shape?

explain.say: Even the name is modest: sonnet comes from the Italian sonetto, a little sound or little song. Today Terrance Hayes writes sonnets that drop rhyme altogether but keep the fourteen-line pressure. Brilliant work. Challenge: write fourteen lines about your morning, with a turn at line nine.

faq.a: A poem of fourteen lines, traditionally in iambic pentameter in English, with a set rhyme scheme and a turn in thought. The main types are the Petrarchan, or Italian, and the Shakespearean, or English.
It is usually credited to Giacomo da Lentini, a poet at the court of Emperor Frederick II in Sicily in the thirteenth century. Petrarch made it famous across Europe a century later.
asks: Where did the sonnet come from?

faq.q: Who brought the sonnet to English?
faq.a: Sir Thomas Wyatt and Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, in the early sixteenth century, translating and imitating Petrarch. Surrey developed the three-quatrains-and-couplet form that Shakespeare later used.

The turn in a sonnet where the argument, mood or perspective shifts. In a Petrarchan sonnet it usually comes at line nine; in a Shakespearean sonnet it often comes at line nine or with the final couplet.

faq.q: Why did English poets change the rhyme scheme?
faq.a: English has far fewer rhyming words than Italian, so finding four or five words on the same rhyme for an octave is hard. Using seven different rhyme sounds made the form work in English.
asks: Why is the English sonnet different?

facts: The sonnet is usually credited to Giacomo da Lentini at the Sicilian court of Frederick II in the thirteenth century.
Wyatt's and Surrey's sonnets were first printed in Tottel's Miscellany in 1557.
